# The microbial world

> *Most living things are too small to see, and most of those cause no harm. Microbes differ in size
> and in how they are related to each other and to us, and only some of them have been proved to
> cause disease.*

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Learning objectives
- Place infectious agents in order of size, and explain what size means for seeing them and for how
  fast they grow.
- Distinguish prions, viruses, bacteria, fungi, protozoa and helminths by what they are built from.
- Explain why a bacterium is easier to attack without harming the patient than a fungus or a
  protozoan.
- State Koch's postulates, and explain why many real pathogens fail them.
- Use the six questions to compare a bacterium, a virus, a fungus, a protozoan and a helminth.
:::

## What microbes are {#sec-world-what}

### A matter of scale {#sec-world-scale}

A **microorganism**, or microbe, is any living thing too small to see without a microscope. The term
covers bacteria, archaea, fungi such as yeasts, and **protozoa**, single-celled eukaryotes that move
and feed independently. Viruses are usually included, although they are not cells. Medical
microbiology also covers **helminths** (parasitic worms), most of which are visible to the naked eye,
because they too are infectious agents.

Try putting these in order of size before reading on.

<div data-island="rank-order" data-src="/diagrams/size-ladder.yml"></div>

Size sets what a microscope can show. A light microscope cannot separate two points closer than
about 0.2 µm, its limit of **resolution**, so stained bacteria are visible but viruses are not.
Viruses were first seen in the late 1930s with the electron microscope, and in clinical practice they
are usually detected through their nucleic acid or their proteins.

Size also favours fast growth. A small cell has a large surface area for its volume, so nutrients
reach every part of it quickly by diffusion.

::: {.example}
In good conditions *Escherichia coli* can divide every 20 minutes, while human cells take many hours.
:::

### Six kinds of infectious agent {#sec-world-kinds}

Six kinds of agent cause infection in humans. Four are cells and two are not:

::: {.concept-tree}
[Kinds of infectious agent]{.tree-title}

- Cells
  - Prokaryotes, with no nucleus
    - Bacteria
  - Eukaryotes, with a nucleus
    - Fungi
    - Protozoa
    - Helminths
- Not cells
  - Viruses: a genome in a protein coat
  - Prions: a misfolded protein with no genome
:::

All cellular life falls into three **domains**, defined by comparing the genes for ribosomal RNA
[@woese1990domains]. Bacteria are **prokaryotes**, cells with no nucleus and no membrane-bound
organelles. Archaea are also prokaryotes, but their membranes and enzymes differ so much from those
of bacteria that they form a separate branch; some live in the human gut, but none is an established
cause of human disease. Eukarya are organisms whose cells have a nucleus. Fungi, protozoa and
helminths belong here, alongside human cells.

A bacterium has many structures that human cells lack, so it is relatively easy to attack without
harming the patient. A fungus or a protozoan shares most of its machinery with human cells, which
leaves fewer safe targets. We can therefore expect the answer to the question *what does it have that
my cells lack?* to differ sharply between domains.

Two kinds of agent sit outside the tree of life. **Viruses** are not cells: a virus particle, or
**virion**, is a genome of DNA or RNA inside a protein coat, sometimes wrapped in a lipid envelope, and
it can be copied only inside a living cell. **Prions** have no genome at all. A prion is a misfolded
form of a normal host protein that converts other copies of the protein into the misfolded shape,
causing fatal neurodegenerative disease after an incubation period that can last years. Prions are
rare, but they matter in practice because routine sterilisation does not reliably inactivate them
([*Detecting and controlling microbes*](detection-control.qmd#sec-det-control)).

Sort the descriptions below by their traits. None of them names the agent.

## Microbes and disease {#sec-world-disease}

### Most microbes are harmless {#sec-world-harmless}

A **pathogen** is a microbe that can cause disease. Pathogens are a small minority of the microbial
world: about 1,400 species are known to infect humans [@taylor2001risk], out of millions of microbial
species, and most of those 1,400 cause disease only in some people, some of the time.

Far more microbes live alongside humans without causing harm. The human body carries about
3.8 × 10^13^ bacteria, mostly in the colon, against about 3.0 × 10^13^ human cells
[@sender2016cells]. These resident communities are the **microbiota** (see [*Microbes and their
hosts*](host-microbe.qmd#sec-host-microbiota)).

::: {.callout-important}
## Do bacteria outnumber human cells ten to one?
This figure is still widely quoted. It came from a rough 1970s estimate that assumed every gram of
the gut contained as many bacteria as a gram of faeces. A careful recount in 2016 put the ratio at
about 1.3 bacteria for every human cell, and a single bowel movement can shift it noticeably
[@sender2016cells].
:::

Some microbes are directly useful to medicine:

- The first recombinant human insulin, approved in 1982, was made by *E. coli* carrying synthetic
  genes for the two insulin chains.
- Many antibiotics were first found as products of soil bacteria.
- In Singapore, *Wolbachia*, a bacterium that lives inside the cells of many insects, is being used
  against dengue.

::: {.example}
Male *Aedes aegypti* mosquitoes carrying *Wolbachia* are released in large numbers; when they mate
with wild females, the eggs do not hatch, so the population of the mosquito that transmits dengue
falls. In a cluster-randomised trial in Singapore, the releases reduced the odds of
laboratory-confirmed dengue by about 70% [@lim2026wolbachia].
:::

### How microbes came to be blamed {#sec-world-history}

Until the late nineteenth century most doctors attributed epidemics to bad air, or **miasma**, and to
imbalances within the body. The **germ theory of disease**, the principle that specific microbes cause
specific diseases, was assembled from several lines of work.

| When | Who | What it showed |
|---|---|---|
| 1670s | Antonie van Leeuwenhoek | Microbes exist: he described "animalcules" seen through his hand-made lenses |
| 1840s | Ignaz Semmelweis | Hand washing with chlorinated lime cut deaths from fever after childbirth ([*Transmission, outbreaks and One Health*](transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-semmelweis)) |
| 1860s | Louis Pasteur | Microbes cause fermentation and do not arise spontaneously in sterile broth |
| 1867 | Joseph Lister | Carbolic acid on wounds and instruments reduced post-operative infection |
| 1876–1882 | Robert Koch | *Bacillus anthracis* causes anthrax, and *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* causes tuberculosis |

Koch's group also set out the logic for proving that a microbe causes a disease. In the form usually
taught, **Koch's postulates** require that:

1. The organism is found in every case of the disease.
2. It can be isolated and grown in pure culture.
3. The cultured organism causes the disease when introduced into a healthy, susceptible host.
4. The same organism can be recovered from that host.

The postulates remain a sound way to think about causation, but many real pathogens fail them:

- Some cannot be grown on laboratory media at all.
- Many cause disease in only some of the people they infect, so there are healthy **carriers**:
  people who harbour and can transmit the organism without being ill.
- Others need a particular host factor, or cause disease only together with other microbes.

Modern versions of the postulates work with genes rather than whole organisms: a gene is linked to
the organism's capacity to cause disease if inactivating it reduces disease and restoring it brings
the disease back [@falkow1988molecular].

## Same questions, different answers {#sec-world-questions}

### The anchor organisms {#sec-world-anchors}

The examples in the foundation chapters, and in the opening chapters of each world, come from eleven
anchor organisms:

| Organism | Kind of agent | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| *Staphylococcus aureus* | Bacterium | A spherical bacterium that many healthy people carry in the nose |
| *Streptococcus pyogenes* | Bacterium | A spherical bacterium carried in the throat of some healthy people; a common cause of sore throat |
| *Escherichia coli* | Bacterium | A rod-shaped bacterium of the healthy gut, and a common cause of bladder infection |
| *Bacteroides fragilis* | Bacterium | A rod-shaped bacterium of the healthy colon that cannot grow in air |
| *Mycobacterium tuberculosis* | Bacterium | A slow-growing bacterium with a waxy wall; the cause of tuberculosis |
| *Burkholderia pseudomallei* | Bacterium | A bacterium of soil and surface water; the cause of melioidosis |
| Influenza virus | Virus | An enveloped RNA virus that infects the cells lining the airway |
| Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) | Virus | An enveloped RNA virus that infects cells of the immune system; the cause of AIDS |
| *Candida albicans* | Fungus | A yeast that lives harmlessly on the skin and in the gut and vagina of most people |
| *Plasmodium falciparum* | Protozoan | A single-celled parasite, carried by mosquitoes, that lives in human liver and red blood cells; the most dangerous cause of malaria |
| *Ascaris lumbricoides* | Helminth | A roundworm that lives in the human intestine; its eggs are swallowed from soil |

### Six questions for every agent {#sec-world-six}

The same six questions apply to every kind of microbe:

1. What is it built from?
2. How does it get energy, and what does it need to grow?
3. How does it copy itself and change?
4. Where does it live, and how does it spread?
5. How does damage happen, and how much of it comes from the microbe and how much from the host?
6. What does it have that my cells lack?

The answers differ sharply between kinds of agent:

| | Bacterium (*S. aureus*) | Virus (influenza virus) | Fungus (*C. albicans*) | Protozoan (*P. falciparum*) | Helminth (*A. lumbricoides*) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Built from | Prokaryotic cell with a peptidoglycan wall | RNA genome, protein coat, lipid envelope | Eukaryotic cell with a chitin and glucan wall | Eukaryotic cell, no wall | Multicellular animal |
| Energy | Its own metabolism | None of its own; uses the host cell's | Its own metabolism | Its own metabolism, using host nutrients | Its own metabolism, feeding on gut contents |
| Copying | Binary fission; exchanges genes | Copied inside host cells; genome segments reshuffle | Budding | Asexual cycles in humans, sexual stage in the mosquito | Sexual reproduction; eggs |
| Home and spread | Nose and skin; contact | Airway; respiratory particles | Skin, gut, vagina | Human liver and red cells; mosquito bite | Human intestine; eggs swallowed from soil |
| Damage | Invasion and toxins | Destroys airway cells; host inflammation | Overgrowth when defences fall | Destroys red cells; blocks small vessels | Heavy burdens obstruct the gut and impair nutrition |
| Unlike my cells | Peptidoglycan wall; 70S ribosomes | Viral enzymes for copying its genome | Ergosterol in its membrane; chitin and glucan wall | Its own folate synthesis (human cells take folate from the diet) | Worm-specific nerve and muscle ion channels |
